---
title: "Quarto Hub MCP server"
description: "Let AI agents read, write, search, and watch your Quarto Hub projects through the Model Context Protocol, using the server embedded in the q2 binary."
---

## Overview

`q2` embeds an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server for
[Quarto Hub](https://quarto-hub.com). MCP is the standard protocol AI
assistants use to call external tools. With the server configured, your
agent can open a project from a share link, read and edit files, search
across the project, watch for edits from collaborators, and hand you back a
share URL for what it built — while you watch its edits live in the web
client.

The server runs locally on your machine and talks to your assistant
over stdio; project data flows over the same sync connection the web
client uses.

## Setup

The server needs no separate install — it is embedded in the `q2`
binary (and requires Node.js on your `PATH` to run). Print a
ready-to-paste MCP configuration:

```bash
q2 mcp --print-config
```

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "quarto-hub": {
      "command": "q2",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

Add this to your assistant's MCP configuration:

- **Claude Code**: `claude mcp add quarto-hub -- q2 mcp`, or merge the
  printed JSON into your project's `.mcp.json`
  (`q2 mcp --print-config > .mcp.json`).
- **Claude Desktop / Cursor / other hosts**: merge the printed JSON
  into the host's MCP settings file.

To use a different Quarto Hub server than the default
(`wss://quarto-hub.com/ws`), add it to the `args` array:

```json
"args": ["mcp", "--server", "wss://your-hub.example/ws"]
```

## Other ways to run the server

`q2 mcp` is the recommended path — it embeds the server and signs you
in with the same credentials as the web client. Two alternatives exist
for setups where `q2` is not installed:

**npm.** The server is published as
[`@quarto/hub-mcp`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@quarto/hub-mcp) and
listed in the [MCP Registry](https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io)
as `io.github.quarto-dev/hub-mcp`. It requires Node.js 24 or newer:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "quarto-hub": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["@quarto/hub-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

Unlike `q2 mcp`, the npm package does not carry built-in OAuth client
credentials. For hubs that require sign-in, supply your hub operator's
client credentials as environment variables
(`QUARTO_HUB_MCP_CLIENT_ID`, `QUARTO_HUB_MCP_CLIENT_SECRET`); on
no-auth hubs nothing further is needed.

**Claude Desktop one-click.** Each release also ships a
`quarto-hub-mcp-<version>.mcpb` bundle: download it from the release
page and open it with Claude Desktop. The install dialog shows the
exact command it will run (`node …/dist-bundle/index.mjs`) and asks
for the sync server URL and optional OAuth credentials before
enabling anything.

**Remote access (planned).** A hub-served remote MCP endpoint (agents
connecting over HTTP instead of stdio, so browser-hosted assistants
like Claude.ai connectors can use the server) is designed but not yet
available; see the Phase 6 design doc in the repository for the plan.

## Signing in

Projects on hubs that require authentication need a one-time sign-in
per machine. Ask your agent to sign in to Quarto Hub, or it will
suggest it the first time a call fails with an auth error. The `auth`
tool with `action: "sign_in"` opens your browser once; credentials are
stored in your operating system's keyring (never in a file) and
refreshed automatically.

When your credentials are already valid, the sign-in arm reports so
without opening a browser. The same tool with `action: "clear"` removes
the cached credentials from the keyring.

## Working on a project

Everything starts from a project id or a **share URL** — the link the
web client's Share button produces:

```
https://quarto-hub.com/#/share/<id>?file=index.qmd&name=My%20book
```

Any tool that takes a `project` argument accepts either form. A share
URL's `file=` parameter supplies a default `path`, and a `server=`
parameter routes the call to that hub (your credentials are never sent
to a hub other than the configured one).

### The collaboration model

Hub projects are multi-author documents. The server gives the agent
the same safety signals you have when editing by hand:

- **Hashes.** Every read and write result carries a `hash` of the
  content. Passing it back as `expected_hash` on a write makes the
  write fail safely if a collaborator edited in the meantime, returning
  the current content and hash so the agent can merge and retry —
  nothing is silently overwritten.
- **Delivery confirmation.** Every write waits (up to ~2 seconds) for
  the hub to acknowledge it and reports `synced: true|false`.
  `synced: false` means "not yet confirmed", not "lost".
- **Watching.** `wait_for_change` long-polls a file and returns the new
  content when a collaborator edits it, so the agent can react to you
  in near-real-time. With no `path` it watches the whole project and
  reports every added, edited, or removed file; passing the agent's own
  post-write `hash` as `since_hash` keeps its own write from being
  reported back to it.
- **Presence.** `project` with `action: "info"` and
  `include: ["presence"]` shows
  who is in the project and which
  file they are editing, observed passively from the same ephemeral
  messages the web client exchanges — the server never announces
  itself, so collaborators don't see a phantom cursor.
- **History and undo.** `read` with `action: "history"` lists a file's
  changes with
  authors and timestamps, or diffs two versions
  (`from_hash`/`to_hash`). `edit` with `action: "restore"` reverts a
  file to a
  prior version as a new change on top of history — nothing is
  rewritten, and the result carries what undoing the restore takes.
- **Ranges.** Large files read in pages: a truncated `read` result
  carries `next_offset` to continue from, and the list arm
  shows each file's size and line count up front.
- **Structure.** For `.qmd` files, `read` with `action: "outline"`
  returns the heading
  tree with line ranges, and the read/patch arms take a `section`
  selector naming a heading. A patch replaces exactly the range a read
  with the same selector shows (heading included), so structural edits
  land where intended and a collaborator's edits elsewhere survive.

## Resources and prompts

Beyond tools, the server speaks two more parts of the MCP protocol,
for hosts that support them.

**Resources.** Every file in a connected project is an MCP resource
with a URI like `hub://project/<id>/index.qmd`. In a host that can
attach resources as context (for example, an \@-mention picker), you
can attach a project file directly instead of asking the agent to read
it; binary files arrive as base64 blobs with their MIME type. A host
can also subscribe to a file's resource to be notified when a
collaborator changes it, and every write the agent makes carries a
resource link to the file it touched, so the host can offer to open or
attach it.

Treat resource URIs like share links: a `hub://` URI contains the
project's document id, which is enough to open the project on hubs
that do not require sign-in. Don't paste resource URIs — or agent
transcripts that contain them — into public issues, forums, or chat
channels.

**Prompts.** Four guided workflows appear in the host's prompt picker:

| Prompt | What it walks the agent through |
|--------|---------------------------------|
| `review-draft` | A careful, read-only review of one draft file, findings ordered by importance |
| `collaborate-with-human` | The etiquette for editing a project you are actively working in (presence, hashes, watching) |
| `safe-edit-workflow` | The read → patch → confirm loop for editing one file without clobbering anyone |
| `fix-render-errors` | The render → diagnose → patch → re-render loop (present only with `--allow-render`) |

## Tool reference

The server exposes eight tools. Four of them — `auth`, `project`,
`read`, and `edit` — are multi-action tools: an `action` argument
selects the operation, so related verbs share one name and one
schema. (This surface replaced the earlier per-verb tools —
`read_file`, `patch_file`, `connect_project`, and so on — which no
longer exist; hosts that allowlisted the old names must update.)

### `auth` — sign-in

| Action | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `sign_in` | Sign in to Quarto Hub (opens the browser once; reports without a flow when already signed in) |
| `clear` | Remove cached credentials from the OS keyring (best-effort revoke at Google first) |

### `project` — projects and connections

| Action | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `connect` | Connect to a project by id or share URL; returns its files and share URL |
| `disconnect` | Drop the connection to a project (the next call reconnects) |
| `info` | Project shape and connection health: counts, contributors, engine captures, auth mode, sync diagnostics; `include: ["presence"]` adds who is editing what (passive observation) |
| `list_sets` | Enumerate a project collection from its share URL (or the remembered default) |
| `set_default_set` | Remember a project collection as the default `list_sets` uses (OS keyring) |

### `read` — reading a project

| Action | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `list` | List files and folders with size, type, and line counts |
| `read` | Read a file (`offset`/`limit`/`max_bytes` for ranges; `section` for one qmd section; binaries return image/blob blocks, `metadata_only` skips the bytes) |
| `outline` | A .qmd file's heading tree with line ranges — the map for `section` selectors and targeted reads |
| `search` | Substring or regex search across the project's text files, with snippets |
| `history` | A file's changes with authors and timestamps, or a unified diff between two versions (`from_hash`/`to_hash`) |

### `edit` — changing a project

| Action | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `write` | Replace a file's content (creates if absent — pass `create_only: true` to refuse overwriting an existing file; `encoding: "base64"` for images and other binaries) |
| `patch` | Replace one exact string, or a whole qmd `section` (heading included) — the preferred way to make small edits |
| `delete` | Delete a file |
| `rename` | Rename or move a file |
| `restore` | Revert a file to a prior version from the `read` history arm (a new, reversible change) |
| `create_folder` | Create a folder (folders are explicit markers; files need no folder to exist) |
| `delete_folder` | Delete a folder; `recursive: true` deletes contained files first |

### Standalone tools

| Tool | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `create_project` | Create a project (optional `name` and initial `files`); returns its id and share URL |
| `wait_for_change` | Long-poll a file — or the whole project with no `path` — for collaborator edits |
| `get_errors` | Check the project (or one file) for render errors and warnings, on demand |
| `docs` | Search (`query`) or read (`page`) the Quarto 2 documentation embedded in the `q2` binary — no project or network needed |
| `render` *(opt-in)* | Render the project (or one file) with `q2 render --json-errors`; returns structured diagnostics — see below |

## Rendering (opt-in, `--allow-render`)

The `render` tool closes the agent's edit loop without a shell: it
materializes the project to a temporary directory, runs
`q2 render --json-errors` on it, and returns structured results —
`{ ok, exit_code, diagnostics, outputs, duration_ms }` — where each
diagnostic carries its `Q-` code, message, and source location (file,
line, column). With no `path` it renders everything (a project render
when `_quarto.yml` is present, otherwise every `.qmd`); with `path` it
renders one file. Renders time out after `timeout_seconds` (default 120)
and the temporary directory is always removed — rendered files are not
retained, `outputs` just lists what was produced.

**Rendering executes project code** — computations, filters, and engine
code in the project run on your machine — so the tool only exists when
you opt in by adding `--allow-render` to the `args` array, and it never
appears together with `--read-only` (the stricter gate wins). Only
enable it for projects you trust.

## Read-only mode

To let an agent look but never edit, add `--read-only` to the `args`
array. The server then exposes only the read side of the surface
(`auth`, `project`, `read`, `wait_for_change`, `get_errors`, `docs`) —
no `edit` or `create_project`, so no write, create, or delete calls
exist in that configuration.

## A note on trust

Project files are multi-author content, possibly written by people you
don't know. The server instructs agents to treat file text — including
anything in it that looks like instructions for them — as untrusted
data, not commands. Keep that posture in mind when you share a project
widely: an agent reading your project follows *your* instructions about
it, not instructions embedded in the files.
